title: Clear contracts

lines: A PRICE FOR THE WHOLE CROP.
cards: Spring in an orchard. The date palms have just set their fruit, small and green, nowhere near ready. A buyer walks up and offers the farmer a price for the whole crop, right now.

The farmer could use the cash; the buyer is gambling on a good harvest. Both are adults, both willing. And yet the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, in a report in Sahih al-Bukhari, forbade selling fruit before its ripening shows.
Why stop a deal two people want?

teach.b: Day three hundred eighty-eight met the verse that opens surah five, in Pickthall's words: "O ye who believe! Fulfil your undertakings." The word he renders undertakings is 'uqud, the plural of 'aqd, a contract.
Since it's addressed to believers, keeping a contract becomes part of faith, not just good business. Today, what the jurists said makes a contract real enough to keep. Three answers.
Near the end of surah two, believers who contract a debt for a fixed term are told to write it down, with a scribe who writes fairly, and witnesses. Paper, so memory can't bend it later.
Second, consent. The Qur'an speaks of trade by mutual agreement, and the jurists hold that a contract made under pressure or trickery doesn't bind the way a free one does.
Third, no excessive uncertainty, called gharar. In Sahih Muslim, the Prophet forbids the sale decided by a thrown pebble and the sale of gharar.
That's the orchard: unripe fruit might become a harvest or nothing, and one side pays for a gamble neither can see.
Excessive, the scholars say, because ordinary deals carry a little uncertainty; you can't know the exact taste of a melon. What's forbidden is the kind that turns a sale into a bet.
Clear words, a free yes, and enough knowledge on both sides: an 'aqd worth keeping.

how: Islamic law asks that contracts be clear, freely agreed and free of excessive uncertainty, and the Qur'an asks that debts with a term be written down with witnesses; Muslim scholars review modern contracts with these conditions in mind.

o: a spoken promise that binds only before God, not in court
a written deed that must be signed before a judge
a contract: clear terms, freely agreed, nothing gambled

p: a debt for a fixed term

s: Islamic law forbids any contract with any uncertainty at all
only excessive uncertainty; ordinary deals carry a little.
the Qur'an tells believers to write down a debt with a fixed term
near the end of surah two, with a fair scribe and witnesses.
a contract made under pressure binds the same as a free one
the jurists require real consent; trade is by mutual agreement.

games.q: you're a farmer. your date palms have just set their fruit, still green. a buyer offers cash for the whole crop today. what does the report in Bukhari say?
o: sell it, since you both agree.
wait until the fruit's ripening shows.
sell it, but only for half the price.
games.why: the Prophet forbade selling fruit before it is clearly fit; until then the sale is a gamble on what neither can see.

practice: Think of something you agreed to lately without really reading it: an app's terms, a lease, a vague promise to a friend.
Ask today's three questions: is it clear what each side gives, was the yes free, is something hidden that neither side could see?
You don't need answers; just notice which of the three is shakiest, and let it rest with your breathing.

wordCard.voice: 'Aqd. A contract, which the Qur'an tells believers to fulfill, made with clear terms, free consent and no excessive uncertainty. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: a contract; its plural 'uqud appears in the opening verse of surah five.
